items.title: Harold Danko interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, April 28, 2021
items.q: I guess like the time with Chet, which was right after Woody Herman, was just the first time I played with him... my Chet Baker association, which went to about 1976 or so

ctx.x: Playing for singers, did that bear fruit when you started playing for Chet Baker and Lee Konitz? They’re both such great melodists.

I guess like the time with Chet, which was right after Woody Herman, was just the first time I played with him, the first few years when I was on the road, I didn’t do the records that he was doing at that point because that was CTI sort of thing that he was involved with so they used Bob James and whoever was the house rhythm section. But that was an education because he sang and played, you know, he did everything. And previous to that I’d done some singers in Ohio. I worked with Maureen McGovern when she was a…

sang just to set the mood basically. That’s the only reason he said he sang. He wanted to set that mood and then kind of retain that mood for those eight minutes or whatever. And that was important for me to understand, to not try to play everything I know on a ballad or something, just like stay there and then let the next tune be its thing too.
